question: The European Court of Auditors has criticised the European Commission for setting overly ambitious or, in other words, unachievable targets for 2030 for the production and use of renewable hydrogen. Furthermore, it considers the Commission’s figures to be driven by political will rather than being based on robust analyses. Employing countless consultants and large companies, the Commission has for years been spending hundreds of millions of taxpayers’ money on this. 1.
How will the Commission respond to the Court’s criticism, and will the targets be lowered or postponed to a later date?

With the Court of Auditors deeming that the Commission’s targets have no chance of actually being achieved, how did the Commission come up with the figures for the quantity of hydrogen to be produced within the EU?
How is it even possible for such serious errors of judgement to occur, and who was responsible in this specific case?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.3.2025) The Commission’s reply to the Court’s observations and recommendations was published alongside the audit1.

The REPowerEU Plan2 suggested an aspirational target of 10 million tonnes of EU renewable hydrogen production and 10 million tonnes of renewable hydrogen imports by 2030 to lower the imports of Russian fossil fuels, proposing to increase the mandatory targets for renewable hydrogen consumption in industry and the transport sector3.

The co-legislators however decided on a lower level of binding targets under the Renewable Energy Directive4. In addition, the co-legislators also agreed on mandatory targets for renewable hydrogen consumption in industry in 2035 and laid out pathways in the aviation5 and maritime6 sector to promote the uptake of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen up to 2050.

The Commission is currently working with Member States, including through an assessment of their National Energy and Climate Plans, to ensure the timely transposition of the mandatory demand volumes decided by the co-legislators in industry and transport.
